sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the HERBERT-ARRAKIS-MEMORIAL sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. Vela receives prescience and sees the safest path become so obvious that every alternative appears irresponsible. The memorial bore the name of Frank Herbert — Dune precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster’s Hunger could no longer be presented as a romantic mystery. It was a pathology of cognitive power: whatever she could completely reduce to a model ceased to appear to her as outside herself. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. 323 At the center of the conflict was Rho, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Orin compares prescience to Aster's illness: too much knowledge can turn freedom into the obligation to execute the model. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Pr — Prescience: an accessible future becomes a political trap; Eg — Empire-Generating Ecology: a local biosphere organizes cosmic politics. Course references included Frank Herbert — Dune. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. 324 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Aster felt the Hunger precisely when an explanation closed too elegantly. A perfect theory reduced surprise, and surprise was the last symptom that something before her had not yet become part of her. The children had noticed that their disagreement calmed her more than any extravagant universe did. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Marae chooses a riskier branch simply to preserve a relationship the optimum would sacrifice. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. No one could now claim that Tern was merely pursuing an obsession. The threshold had a technical address, but access required a deliberate reduction of power. The more extensions of Aster one tried to carry through it, the more the channel closed. Exteriority required leaving something behind. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the COPYING operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — creates a second instance similar enough for continuity to become a problem — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a 325 copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 326 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
